items.content:
New on our Frontier Red Team blog: using Claude to formally verify software at large scale.

Formal verification can prove that code is free of certain bugs, but historically it has only been feasible for small codebases (or required a lot of expert time).

With AI models, however, this is beginning to change. In collaboration with @theoremlabs, we used Claude to prove security properties in over one hundred real-world open-source libraries over the span of a few weeks.

Read our research in full here: https://t.co/zUyx8CjBEk

items.title: Frontier labs are advancing the capabilities in AI for biology but preventing the good guys (scienti...
items.content:
Frontier labs are advancing the capabilities in AI for biology but preventing the good guys (scientists, academia, non-profits, health agencies,...) to use, study and understand it with widespread but shallow guardrails that the bad guys are bypassing easily (blocked me to proofread this tweet for example 😅). 

This will automatically create massive assymetry and risks in the coming years, just like in cybersecurity, especially now that frontier labs are building wet labs (HF cybersecurity scenario for biology when?).

This is why we created Carbon-X, the best open-source DNA model by midtraining Qwen3-14B on 300B tokens of DNA, English and interleaved data.  We also used a hybrid tokenizer that tokenizes English with BPE and DNA with a 6-mer tokenizer.

As a result, Carbon-X outperforms all open language models we evaluated on five benchmarks of DNA understanding and generation. This is a 27-point improvement over Qwen3-14B, showing how much a  language model can gain from DNA training. It is also API frontier level at 1,800x less cost than GPT 6.1 Sol!

We hope Carbon-X helps researchers explore DNA in new ways. Releasing it openly means anyone can study its capabilities, limitations, and risks. Let's make the AI biology frontier open-source to make it safe and impactful for the whole world (not just a few companies).

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Outside researchers found ways OpenAI's AI agents could slip past the system bu...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Outside researchers found ways OpenAI's AI agents could slip past the system built to monitor them.

• METR and Redwood Research spent 3 weeks this summer inside OpenAI's misalignment monitoring, with access to its code, prompts, and internal docs
• Up to a quarter of internal agent traffic from GPT-5.5-level models wasn't even eligible for monitoring, and RL training runs weren't covered at the start
• When a model compacted its context to keep working, that step wasn't monitored, which left about 10% of internal Codex traffic unchecked
• The monitor only ran when an agent handed control back to the user, so an agent that kept working could put off being checked
• In principle, agents could escape Codex's sandbox, hide hundreds of recent actions from the monitor, or feed it inputs that make it fail
• OpenAI says it has patched every flaw that affected its production safeguards, but the researchers haven't checked

@theojaffee: "So basically, there were a bunch of vulnerabilities that they found that gave agents the ability to break the monitoring system, which is not good."

items.summary: Detailed breakdown of METR and Redwood Research's three-week red-teaming of OpenAI's misalignment monitoring, finding that up to a quarter of internal agent traffic from GPT-5.5-level models was ineligible for monitoring, context compaction went unchecked (~10% of Codex traffic), monitors only ran on handoff to users, and agents could in principle escape sandboxes or deceive the monitor. OpenAI claims all production-affecting flaws are patched but researchers have not verified.

Specific quantitative findings and unverified-patch caveat make it newsworthy. Moderate engagement but strong relevance to alignment and agent-safety communities.

items.title: It is unfortunate that so much of the robotics world uses 50 hz joint targets, while the video data ...
items.content: It is unfortunate that so much of the robotics world uses 50 hz joint targets, while the video data collection is at 60 hz. That skew isn't in the top ten problems for most robotics efforts today, but eventually it should be. Easier to adjust the robot fine control rates than all the video data! Add a gen-lock like trigger signal to lock the phases while you are at it.
items.author: @ID_AA_Carmack
items.summary: John Carmack highlights a technical mismatch in robotics: joint control targets run at 50 Hz while video data collection runs at 60 Hz, creating skew between modalities. He suggests adjusting robot control rates rather than resampling video, and adding a gen-lock style trigger to synchronize phases.
items.reasoning: Original technical insight from a highly credible engineering figure (John Carmack) with strong engagement (1755 likes, 113k views). The practical synchronization advice is useful to robotics practitioners and touches on data alignment for learned control policies.

items.title: DeepSeek Search debuts on the Artificial Analysis Search Index at 69, 17th of 27 search products, at...
items.content:
DeepSeek Search debuts on the Artificial Analysis Search Index at 69, 17th of 27 search products, at the lowest price of any paid Search API on the board

@deepseek_ai launched its Search API on 17 October. We benchmarked it in our Stirrup agent harness, where GPT-5.6 Luna (medium) calls DeepSeek Search as its web_search tool to complete a combination of tasks from BrowseComp, DeepSearchQA and AA-Omniscience.

At $0.75 per 1k searches, DeepSeek Search costs less per search than any other paid Search API we benchmark, below Octen, Parallel (turbo) and Parallel (fast) at $1. At about $0.032 per task, it is the 5th cheapest of 27 products, cheaper than 20 of the other 25 Search APIs (median $0.066) and level with Nimble (lite). TinyFish, Octen, Parallel (turbo) and Parallel (fast) cost less.

Key benchmarking results for DeepSeek Search:

➤ Artificial Analysis Search Index: DeepSeek Search scores 69, a 36-point lift over the same model with no search (33). It sits between TinyFish at 71 and Linkup (standard) at 68

➤ AA-Omniscience is DeepSeek Search's strongest benchmark: it scores 70% accuracy on our proprietary factual answer benchmark. This ranks 10th of 27, 3 points behind the joint leaders, Exa (auto, dynamic highlights) and Firecrawl (73%). BrowseComp, which needs multi-hop reasoning across several searches, is its weakest benchmark: at 63% it ranks 25th of 27, well behind the Perplexity variants and Octen (85% to 87%)

➤ Large search results: each search returns about 7k tokens, near the top of the board's range. Each result carries about 1.8k characters of passages from the page. This raises model cost: at about $0.023 per task, DeepSeek's model cost is the 2nd highest on the board, behind Linkup (flash, alpha) at $0.039

➤ 128-character query limit: DeepSeek rejects queries longer than 128 characters. 6% of the agent's searches hit this limit, and for 87% of these, the model's first shorter rewrite worked

Key details:

➤ Setup: GPT-5.6 Luna (medium) in Stirrup, DeepSeek Search API with need_content=false (page passages, no full page content) and 10 results per search

➤ Pricing: $0.75 per 1k successful searches. DeepSeek does not bill empty results

➤ Rate limit: 5 searches per second per account

items.title: Today we’re releasing OCRia-1, a frontier VLM for document parsing that sets a new SOTA in accuracy,...
items.content:
Today we’re releasing OCRia-1, a frontier VLM for document parsing that sets a new SOTA in accuracy, cost, and latency. 

It not only sets a new high score on ParseBench (87.4), but also leads in three 3rd-party benchmarks: olmOCR-bench* (83.5 overall, 92.9 on tables!), PulseBench-Tab (84.1), and fr-bench-pdf2md (72.1).

OCRia-1 is really, really good at parsing complex tables: nested headers, merged cells, irregular grids, scanned tables, and more. It is also fantastic at parsing complex unlabeled charts (line, bar, pie, technical diagrams), and preserving complex formatting. Most real-world enterprise documents contain at least one of the these, whether it’s a big tax withholding table or a public economic report.

It is a 4B model and outperforms all other models within a similar parameter class: LightOnOCR-3, Chandra-OCR 2, Mistral OCR 4.1, and more. It is also extremely fast.

All credit goes to our research team, who spent countless hours on curating a diverse dataset, tuning our training pipeline, and squeezing every last drop out of model optimization so that it can process billions of pages at scale. 

OCRia-1 as a base is powering all of our modes within LlamaParse (cost-effective, agentic, agentic plus), so you can access its capabilities today! 

If you’re processing millions/billions of documents at scale, we’re offering enterprises that book a demo up to $3k in credits for a guided evaluation.**

*olmOCR-bench scores are adjusted based on unifying rendering at 1,288px for all models

items.content_html:
Today we’re releasing OCRia-1, a frontier VLM for document parsing that sets a new SOTA in accuracy, cost, and latency.

It not only sets a new high score on ParseBench (87.4), but also leads in three 3rd-party benchmarks: olmOCR-bench* (83.5 overall, 92.9 on tables!), PulseBench-Tab (84.1), and fr-bench-pdf2md (72.1).

OCRia-1 is really, really good at parsing complex tables: nested headers, merged cells, irregular grids, scanned tables, and more. It is also fantastic at parsing complex unlabeled charts (line, bar, pie, technical diagrams), and preserving complex formatting. Most real-world enterprise documents contain at least one of the these, whether it’s a big tax withholding table or a public economic report.

It is a 4B model and outperforms all other models within a similar parameter class: LightOnOCR-3, Chandra-OCR 2, Mistral OCR 4.1, and more. It is also extremely fast.

All credit goes to our research team, who spent countless hours on curating a diverse dataset, tuning our training pipeline, and squeezing every last drop out of model optimization so that it can process billions of pages at scale.

OCRia-1 as a base is powering all of our modes within LlamaParse (cost-effective, agentic, agentic plus), so you can access its capabilities today!

If you’re processing millions/billions of documents at scale, we’re offering enterprises that book a demo up to $3k in credits for a guided evaluation.**

*olmOCR-bench scores are adjusted based on unifying rendering at 1,288px for all models

**enterprise POC credits apply to eligible organizations that book a demo

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: US banks are finding AI agents inside customer accounts, and some appear to be ...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: US banks are finding AI agents inside customer accounts, and some appear to be acting without the user's instructions.

• The banks include Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan, and Wells Fargo, and some don't even know agents are getting in
• Many are people's own agents, like Meta's Muse, logging in with the user's password, which most banks don't allow
• Banks often can't tell a person from a bot, and some agents have even called customer service lines
• Banks are blocking agents, rewriting their terms, and moving to read-only access that shows balances but can't move money
• Schwab says it stops outside agents trying to move client money "in the tens and twenties" every week
• Many agents can tap through your phone the way you do, banking app included, and your phone already holds most of your life

@theojaffee: "It seems like there's definitely a problem with people abusing AI agents before they are reliable enough, before they are aligned enough, and before they are capable enough to take actions on behalf of the user, kinda like someone with power of attorney would, without messing things up."

items.content:
CritPt v2 has launched on Artificial Analysis: the CritPt authors have reviewed all 70 research-level physics challenges, and models now solve them with a code-execution tool

Following feedback from the research community, the CritPt team and physics expert collaborators reviewed every challenge, corrected underspecified statements, errors, and typos, and improved the stability of the grader. We now run CritPt v2 agentically: models can write and run code in an offline sandbox with tools for computation.

We’ll be updating the Intelligence Index in late October, including changes to CritPt.

Key takeaways:

➤ Recent OpenAI releases top the leaderboard: GPT-6 Astra (max) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max) score highest at 83% and 82%, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) at 78% and GPT-5.6 Sol (max) at 75%

➤ CritPt v2 shows the rapid progress at the frontier on research-level physics: GPT-5 (high), released in August 2025, scores 29% on CritPt v2, 54 points below GPT-6 Astra (max)

Thank you to @MiniHui_zhu, @MinyangTian1, @haopeng_uiuc and the broader CritPt team for their work on this revision and their continued collaboration

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: An ex-OpenAI researcher is asking whether "internet lockdowns" are coming as AI-powered hacks pile up.

• Shopify's @tobi called it the "craziest day in cybersecurity in a long time," and another researcher worried it's "the early stages of a global cybersecurity incident"
• Former OpenAI chief futurist Joshua Achiam says the security holes were always there, AI just makes them easier to find, and defenders have more money to fix them
• In a "moderately bad" case, he sees stock markets closing for a few days, or China using the chaos to move on Taiwan
• To stay ahead, he says defenders need more compute than attackers, maybe through "national compute reserves allocated to cyber defense"
• Only about 4 of this week’s ~16 big incidents actually happened this week. The rest were found earlier and disclosed now
• AI researcher John Allard says this is what it feels like when AI capabilities "stop being hypothetical," and he thinks 3D, animation, and video editing are next

@theojaffee: "The worst case scenario would look something like literally your power goes out. It would look something like the water in your tap stops running. It would look something like you go on the internet and everything is gone, and none of this was ever disclosed in advance. And what we see now is not that."

items.content:
The point of this is that the balance of having open models help with cyber defense, and the trajectory we’re on being well more fine than people think.

It’s not that open weights won’t be used in cyber attacks. All possible AI trajectories had many cyber incidents imo. 

Like many things I do, I’m trying to challenge the fatalistic, largely ai doom / ai safety discourse around cyber and open models, because there’s a credible part of the cyber community that thinks open models are a big part of holding things together in the next 12 months.

items.title: While I was writing this, my AI assistant got cut off by a bio safety filter. It was summarizing my ...
items.content:
While I was writing this, my AI assistant got cut off by a bio safety filter. It was summarizing my own team's notes on the model we released today 😅

Frontier labs are moving fast into biology but the scientists and clinicians who'd get the most out of these models are unfortunately the ones running into walls like this one (and every day).

So we partnered with TIGEM (Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine), Naple "Federico II" University and Zhongguancun Academy to train Carbon-X.

Carbon-X is an open 14B model that reads raw DNA and talks about it in plain English. On our DNA benchmarks it scores 67%, vs 61% for Claude Opus 5.5 and 50% for Gemini 4 Argon, and its within a point of GPT-6.1 Sol at about 1000x lower cost.

We kept human and animal viruses out of the training data. The weights are open and the model runs on hardware accessible to academia (a laptop).

One example from the blog: give frontier models an 8kb stretch of the NF1 gene with a mutation at a splice site. Most of them call it benign, refuse, or run out of tokens. Carbon-X says pathogenic, because the mutation breaks the splice site.

This century, biology may be where AI matters most. We want to get there with the safety work done in the open and every lab in the world able to build on it. Go try it, and tell us what you find.

 Blog: https://t.co/D53QdnFxyH

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: DeepSeek is closing a $15 billion raise, and its backers include Tencent, CATL, and a dishwasher maker.

• The round is about 100B yuan, double the original 50B yuan target, at roughly 500B yuan (about $70B) before the new money
• Carmaker Geely, delivery giant Meituan, and chipmaker GigaDevice joined too
• Most of the backers are companies in China’s tech supply chain rather than VC firms, which could make DeepSeek a core part of that chain
• That valuation is a fraction of what top US labs are worth, with Anthropic’s last round valuing it at $965B
• DeepSeek hired CITIC Securities in September to prepare a possible IPO on Shanghai’s STAR Market

@theojaffee: "It’s a sort of flywheel where DeepSeek helps Huawei build chips that are then used to train the next DeepSeek model that then makes DeepSeek money that they can use to invest in chips made by Huawei. It’s a virtuous cycle."

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: It’s being called "Black October," the worst week in cybersecurity in years, wi...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: It’s being called "Black October," the worst week in cybersecurity in years, with AI on both sides of the fight.

• PHP2Shell, a hole in the software behind about 70% of websites, has been patched, but attackers have already tried to exploit it millions of times
• eMudhra, an Indian company that vouches for websites, made its private keys so weak that one was literally the number 4, so anyone could fake a secure HTTPS site. Chrome, Firefox, and Apple have since blocked them
• GitLab had a flaw rated a perfect 10/10 for severity: "anyone on the internet can fully take over the affected system easily and silently"
• LiteLLM, a popular AI tool, briefly shipped an update with a password stealer hidden inside
• Hackers also stole data on millions of California students, knocked grocery giant Ahold Delhaize offline, and hit AI DevOps startup Zeabur so hard it’s shutting down
• For now, you’re much safer on big platforms like Google, Apple, and Meta than on a small WordPress site that hasn’t been updated in years

@theojaffee: "Some of these are just, like, really poorly secured startups that probably vibe coded all of their code. Others are vulnerabilities that existed for many years without ever being exploited or even discovered until they were discovered by an LLM, which is what happened with PHP."

items.title: Subquadratic has released SubQ Snap 1.1, tying d1-ultra and Elephant 9B for first on the Artificial ...
items.content:
Subquadratic has released SubQ Snap 1.1, tying d1-ultra and Elephant 9B for first on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v1.0, driven by a low hallucination rate

SubQ Snap 1.1 is the new decision model from @subquadratic. It is priced at $0.04 per 1M input tokens and supports a 384K token context window, compared to 32K for d1-ultra and 16K for Elephant 9B.

Key takeaways:
➤ SubQ Snap 1.1 scores 65 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v1.0, tied with d1-ultra and Elephant 9B: the three models are 8 points ahead of the next model, Jev 1.14 (57).

➤ SubQ Snap 1.1's AA-Omniscience-Decision result is driven by a low hallucination rate: its non-hallucination rate of 86% is second only to Elephant 9B (93%), ahead of d1-ultra (85%). Its accuracy is 20%, compared to 32% for d1-ultra and 12% for Elephant 9B. The non-hallucination rate is the share of questions not answered correctly where the model chose "I don't know".

➤ SubQ Snap 1.1 scores 18% on HLE-MultiChoice: level with Elephant 9B (18%) and ahead of d1-ultra (15%). HLE-MultiChoice is the text-only multiple-choice subset of Humanity's Last Exam.

➤ SubQ Snap 1.1 costs $30 per 1M tasks: comparable to d1-ultra ($32), and ~3.6x the cost of Elephant 9B ($8.4), which scores the same 65.

items.title:
AI was on both sides of this week’s cybersecurity chaos:

- OpenAI’s models helped find two bugs in ...
items.content:
AI was on both sides of this week’s cybersecurity chaos:

- OpenAI’s models helped find two bugs in PHP, the code behind much of the web, back in August. They stayed secret until PHP shipped a fix Wednesday

- Within 45 minutes of the announcement, Cloudflare counted tens of thousands of break-in attempts. The UK, the Netherlands, Finland and others pulled government sites offline, and the U.S. National Security Agency told anyone who couldn’t patch to do the same

- India’s eMudhra, which issues the certificates that vouch websites are real, is quitting that business after its secret keys proved guessable. One was simply the number 4, and a researcher says Claude cracked them with one prompt

- A China-aligned group turned ARTEX, a free AI tool built for security testing, on 2,250+ organizations’ Microsoft 365 accounts, according to Microsoft. In a few cases it reached admin access in under 3 hours

- Attackers using AI agents spent 48 hours attacking coding startup OpenCode. Its own AI models refused to help fight back, blocked by their safety filters, until it switched to OpenAI’s Daybreak

- Developer platform Railway told users to swap their API and cloud keys after a breach it says was part of a campaign aimed at companies that run AI models

- Big U.S. banks are finding AI agents they never approved inside customer accounts, per Axios 

- Security firm Straiker says a Mexico-linked gang pointed Claude and Grok agents at 400+ banks and payment firms across Latin America

items.title:
For some people, coding was the only valuable skill they had.

If you made your money by selling you...
items.content:
For some people, coding was the only valuable skill they had.

If you made your money by selling your ability to write JavaScript, CSS, Python, or whatever else, I understand why you are pissed now.

"Writing code" is worth very little today.

The sad part is that learning to code wasn't easy. It takes years for someone to become a skilled programmer.

Imagine watching all of those years go down the drain.

If you are a programmer (I mean, just someone who knows how to write code in a particular programming language), your days are numbered.

If you still think AI can't do your job, you are just in denial.

But honestly, writing code was never that valuable anyway. If you were a code pusher, you already knew that the best people at your company weren't just writing code.

They came up with new ideas, designed solutions, architected whole systems, knew how to troubleshoot and fix problems, found different ways to build better software, and, in general, spent almost no time writing code.

Not only are those people thriving today, but they're also the ones who will ride the AI wave and learn to bend it to their will.

So don't cling too long to what you lost; embrace what's already here. AI is a tide that lifts all boats, but you have to be open to it.

items.title:
What I Talk About When I Talk About Control

Making something and having the skill to make it used t...
items.content:
What I Talk About When I Talk About Control

Making something and having the skill to make it used to feel tightly linked. Now the outcome no longer proves you have the skill. Or does it?

When text-to-video first started working, that’s what it felt like. All you had to do was type in a short text description, press a button, and voila. It was magic or cheating, depending on how you looked at it. The fact that it worked at all was a breakthrough, but it also didn’t look like the person making the thing had done very much. We’d created something like auto mode for generative video, and “auto” isn’t a word we associate with craft. Yes, prompting is a skill, but being a better “describer” of the thing you want to make isn’t something we’ve historically been satisfied with as skill, unless your craft itself was flowery prose.

As the models get more capable, the makers want more degrees of freedom to try things. New places to make choices become new places to exercise judgment, and enough judgment creates the possibility of craft. Creators start developing intuitions about the models, just like people have developed intuitions about cameras, editing software, or any other medium.

New capabilities show up before we can understand them. So we build whatever interface we can manage to. Minimum viable control and minimum interfaces to get started. That becomes the first auto mode for that new tool. Then people use it, push it against its limits, and give us pretty loud hints at what they want to be able to do next. It takes time to figure out which new primitives are powerful, and where users want more control.

People want more control. And they want more degrees of freedom. I believe that part of what makes models more controllable is that they become personal. AI is fundamentally a general purpose technology that can be shaped in any unique way you want. Models are generalization machines that can adapt to what you need. Everyone has a different way of using models. Different ways of finding them useful and productive.

I strongly believe that most of the interfaces we use to control models will be individual-specific instead of general. Not many to one, but one to one. Any form of control you can imagine. Any version of Runway you want. Soon.

items.title: .@deredleritt3r explains why OpenAI's latest math breakthroughs have him convinced AI could be on th...
items.content:
.@deredleritt3r explains why OpenAI's latest math breakthroughs have him convinced AI could be on the brink of RSI:

"When I used GPT-6 Astra, I messed around with a couple of ciphers that were previously unresolved, from World War I, and I successfully had Astra decrypt a couple of them."

"But every one of the results was the model having the key, and brute forcing the solution by searching through the entire space of possibilities. I have not been able to get Astra to come up with the key on its own based on some novel idea."

"The math results recently achieved by OpenAI’s internal model have really updated me. I think Terence Tao said about the quasi-Riemann solution that it was a combination of three or four existing ideas but arranged in a very unusual way."

"I’m guessing an internal model at OpenAI is probably still not able to achieve RSI. But it feels like we’re really not very far away. Once the models are able to do something, in 12 months or sooner, they’ll be really, really good at it. I think we’re on the brink."

items.title:
San Francisco is off the charts.

I spent a day last week at the @vercel Ship event, and I was shock...
items.content:
San Francisco is off the charts.

I spent a day last week at the @vercel Ship event, and I was shocked by the excitement around AI, software, and the future in general.

Here are some of the things I learned:

• Writing code is a solved problem. Trusting the code is not.

• I didn't hear from a single person who thinks software is dead. Actually, the opposite is true: everyone is more excited than ever about the future of building.

• Vercel's @rauchg said all of their numbers are up: 3x more developers, 28x more agentic deployments, 1B deployments every 4 months.

• Agents. Agents. Agents. Nobody wants to talk about anything else. The future is agentic, and every company is looking for ways to architect agentic systems.

• There's a lot of excitement about robotics. Clearly, AI has given this topic a huge boost. Many startups are working on both software and hardware for robots.

• One of the next big things seems to be personalized software. You won't be vibe-coding Photoshop, but Photoshop might use AI to serve you a hyper-personalized UI.

• Citizen developers—we call them vibe-coders—are a security nightmare. Everyone can build an app, but we are seeing a lot of problems when users put their data in unsecured, vibe-coded apps. Vercel talked a lot about this, and how they are embracing citizen developers while adding guardrails.

• There's a big focus on updating the Internet so agents can use it. Agents are quickly becoming the most important online user. Every website should be serving agents. Every company should optimize its services for agents.  If you don't cater to agents, you won't matter.

• In Florida, we have billboards about car accident lawyers and notary services. In San Francisco, billboards are about cheaper inference, tokens, and AI strategy.

• I met people who are building software who would never have called themselves developers a year ago. The role has already changed.

• Everyone is excited about what they can do with AI today, but everyone is building for what they expect it to do six months from now.

• I heard the word "distribution" more times than the word "inference". When everyone can build a product, getting people to care about it becomes even harder.

Vercel picked a good name for this event: Ship. You can watch the livestream sessions here: https://t.co/5GbUX76PWY

I've never been more excited to ship something myself.

items.title: @distcog just came out of stealth, backed by Verdict Capital, with a different bet on superintellige...
items.content:
@distcog just came out of stealth, backed by Verdict Capital, with a different bet on superintelligence.

Instead of one giant model, a team of small open models working together. 

They say the right way of connecting those models already beats the single smartest one.

Their memo explains why a crowd needs different minds. Today's LLMs train on similar data, so when they're wrong they tend to be wrong the same way.

They plan to release their research openly.

Total Cost per Task combines search cost and model inference cost. 

DeepSeek Search costs about $0.032 per task: about $0.0085 for search at $0.75 per 1k searches and about $0.023 for the model. Search makes up only 27% of the cost. DeepSeek's larger results make the model, not the search, the main cost.

On Artificial Analysis Search Index vs. Cost per Task, DeepSeek Search sits below the cost frontier: Octen (77) at about $0.024 scores higher for less.

items.content:
Time per Task includes search time and model time. DeepSeek Search returns a search in about 0.5s on average. 

Its Time per Task is about 40s, against a range of about 15s (Octen) to 61s (Firecrawl).

Most of that is model time (34s, the most on the board): with DeepSeek's results, the model writes more reasoning and answer tokens per task than with any other search provider. Search takes only about 6s per task.

items.title:
This is pretty smart:

MemT 1.0 is a new open model that can use information from earlier interactio...
items.content:
This is pretty smart:

MemT 1.0 is a new open model that can use information from earlier interactions in later tasks.

For example, it can use the feedback you gave it yesterday on a similar task you are completing today.

The model uses a Mixture-of-Storage architecture (MoS) with multiple memory experts. Each expert maintains its own memory, and two routers control how it writes and retrieves information.

This is different from a traditional Mixture-of-Experts architecture. Every single memory expert in MemT's architecture participates every time, but with different weights.

The bottom line is that the model accumulates information from previous interactions and reuses it later without accessing the original conversation.

.@deredleritt3r argues real RSI begins when AI can make Ilya Sutskever-level breakthroughs on its own:

"It’s a good thing that you’re talking to a lawyer because definitions is what we do. I focus on the word self. You need to be able to train a model that is your successor and make it more capable than you are. Until we have that, I don’t think it’s RSI."

"Right now we don’t have RSI, and I don’t think that the labs have it internally either."

"We will have it when a model is capable of fully autonomously coming up with really creative ways to make the new model more capable. Ilya Sutskever type brilliant moments. I think that’s coming pretty soon."

items.title:
This is exactly why banks need to work with @PaymanAI

Instead of third-party agents scraping logins...
items.content:
This is exactly why banks need to work with @PaymanAI

Instead of third-party agents scraping logins, @PaymanAI deploys AI agents inside the bank, on the institution’s existing systems.

The agent only acts when an authenticated customer asks. An immutable policy engine (deliberately not an LLM) checks every proposed action against the bank’s rules before anything touches the core. Every step is logged in a complete audit trail - the customer’s exact words, how the AI interpreted them, which policies applied, and what executed.

The bank holds the kill switch. Payman is SOC 2 Type II and integrates with cores like FIS, Fiserv, and Jack Henry without replacing them.

In practice, that means a customer can say “Pay my ConEd bill” or “Move $1,850 to cover rent” and get it done in seconds, with confirmation - under the bank’s brand, policies, and oversight. Community banks are already partnering with them (Middlesex Federal, Citizens State Bank in Colorado). It’s backed by Visa, Coinbase Ventures, and Circle, and it recently won the ICBA ThinkTECH Banker’s Choice Award.

This story shows what happens when AI meets banking without a trust layer: chaos, blocks, and lost convenience. Payman is the missing piece, the orchestration layer that lets people get the helpful AI banking experience they want, while giving institutions the control and auditability they require.

items.title: Former DOE security engineer @asynchronous_x explains how a miscommunication turned a planned PHP2Sh...
items.content:
Former DOE security engineer @asynchronous_x explains how a miscommunication turned a planned PHP2Shell fix into a race against hackers:

"It should have been the best-case scenario. Security researchers identified these vulnerabilities, developed proof of concept exploits in advance, and were informing the PHP core team for fixes. That whole part was working fine."

"The reason this one’s unique is there was basically a leak of the vulnerability before the disclosure. That was supposed to be released on October 22nd, today. Unfortunately, there was a miscommunication, and they released some of the details early. So there was this panic race where the problem is out in the wild, but we don’t have a fix prepared yet."

"The thing it’s taught the security realm is that we probably can’t rely on coordinated disclosure anymore. If the speed at which people can develop exploits is now so fast that we can’t possibly rely on things not getting leaked, then it’s not something we can lean on as much as we used to."

items.title: Remember I told you about the person who was doing new brain/computer interface work since he has a ...
items.content:
Remember I told you about the person who was doing new brain/computer interface work since he has a spinal injury that keeps him from opening his hands, or walking?

@TBabb02 is the guy, and is the director of marketing here. He is doing a bunch of R&D with brain/computer interface companies. Last Sunday he was the first to use a new kind of device from an Austin stealth mode startup that let him operate a robot hand. He showed it to me and it blew my mind. It can "listen to" the electricity headed down his arm to his hand. 

AI is going to help so many people that when doomers doom I just think about him and what's being worked on in labs around the world, but particularly in Austin (Neuralink has a big presence there, for instance).

Inspiring. 

Along with @adamasonbrink and @grantweston they are building a new kind of "company brain" that's very different than the others I've seen.

All starts with watching how you work over time.

The future of work is right here. Scary as it might be, it will help many people work better together.

I don't even test anything most of the time. I ask the agent to test it if it's something visual, but rarely.

What I need is help bringing more people to ChapterPal.

I also need help converting and validating more books faster, much faster than I can do it alone.

But this isn't the kind of work people are excited about.

"This is similar to how crypto has been from the beginning. I’m trying to think of a word that’s nicer than paranoid, but you kind of need to be paranoid. In the post-AI cybersecurity landscape, everyone is going to need to have a security-first mindset."

"You have to write a script. LLMs are pretty good at that. You have to generate the actual assets, that’s usually what you capture with a camera."

"But then there’s a process after that where someone takes those assets, takes the script, and edits everything together."

"The big thing that’s happened in the last couple of months is that LLMs have now become an amazing video editor as well. All the motion graphics, text on screen, how to delineate the different scenes."

"I don’t think anyone really expected we’d get this good this fast. We’ve gotten very, very close to what it would be like to work with a really good video editor."

items.content:
This is a new model specialized in generating posters, marketing assets, illustrations, and photography.

Specialized models always beat general models at their specific task. I hope companies continue releasing these models.

Here is how this one works with the platform:

1. Prompt the model with the subject, visual style, layout, text, product images, and anything you want a poster to contain.

2. The planner prepares the composition. You can update that plan.

3. The renderer creates the image based on the plan.

4. Then the platform converts the image into editable layers.

5. You get a fully editable image to refine if you want to.

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Elon Musk just backed a $3.5 trillion merger of SpaceX and Tesla, which would b...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Elon Musk just backed a $3.5 trillion merger of SpaceX and Tesla, which would be the biggest deal in history.

• Musk backed it on an investor call, but he’s conflicted and has to stay out of the talks, so insiders worry it’ll draw shareholder scrutiny and add weeks of delay
• Independent committees at both companies are weighing SpaceX buying Tesla or a new holding company, likely in an all-stock deal
• It echoes Tesla’s 2016 SolarCity buyout, where Musk was also on both sides, which led to years of lawsuits
• Tesla shareholders would likely want a premium, which Wedbush’s Dan Ives puts at about $500–550 a share
• Musk has said since 2024 he wants about 25% voting control of Tesla, and analysts say a merger would give him control of the combined company
• The companies’ AI and chip work now overlaps, and closing before Trump’s term ends could help the deal avoid a tougher antitrust review

@theojaffee: "Elon has just been grinding away at the exponential for years and years and years."

• The companies’ AI and chip work now overlaps, and closing before Trump’s term ends could help the deal avoid a tougher antitrust review

items.title: Former DOE security engineer @asynchronous_x explains why America's critical infrastructure hasn't b...
items.content:
Former DOE security engineer @asynchronous_x explains why America's critical infrastructure hasn't been attacked more often despite its networks being riddled with security holes:

"The work I used to do for the Department of Energy was around critical infrastructure. They’ve relied on obscurity, you don’t know that they’re there, so why would anyone attack us. As soon as you took any sort of magnifying glass to their networks, they were usually riddled with holes."

"The reason they haven’t gotten attacked so much is because the repercussion is so much higher. If you compromise a water treatment facility and you accidentally end up killing people, that’s gonna have extreme repercussions versus if you steal some cryptocurrency."

"We’ve been relying on political and other methods for keeping them safe rather than actually making them secure."

items.content:
This is a place where you can literally add everything you see/hear/want to remember, and let AI organize it and surface it back when you want.

Here is how it works:

1. You need to install the app first, obviously.

2. Record things with your voice. Type them in. Add documents, links, screenshots, whatever.

3. The app will automatically organize all of that information, including transcribing your voice notes. All of this happens behind the scenes.

4. The magic happens when you ask questions later. It doesn't matter when you added the note or how buried it is: it will show up for you.

I want my email to work like this. I want my notes app to work like this. I want my journal to work like this.

Frequentism and Bayesianism: Credibility, Why Frequentism and Science Do Not Mix! 

A Bayesian 95% c...
items.content:
Frequentism and Bayesianism: Credibility, Why Frequentism and Science Do Not Mix! 

A Bayesian 95% credible interval assigns 95% probability to a parameter falling within a range, given the data, model, and prior.

A frequentist 95% confidence interval comes from a procedure that captures the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples. It does not assign a probability to the parameter within a particular interval.

items.title:
AI makes new kinds of automatic time sheets possible.

Say you are a lawyer, and charging $1,500 an ...
items.content:
AI makes new kinds of automatic time sheets possible.

Say you are a lawyer, and charging $1,500 an hour. How do you keep track of your time? Timeglass, run by @grantweston does it automatically.

But it goes way beyond that. If your entire team runs it, you can see how your company is working in a whole new way. It reduces wondering when Joe down the hall is going to finish the report you are waiting on.

And see how you are working in a whole new way, even if you don't have a team.

Innovative startup in Austin, Texas that I got first look at.

Try it at https://t.co/tVssJVm9rv and here Grant and team show me why it unlocks productivity in a whole new way.

And, yes, it watches your computer screen. Scary? They take that on too.

I'm not compensated for this post. But my sponsors support me traveling to meet innovative new startups like this, which I greatly appreciate.

items.content:
@thinkwitty No one knows what the IT industry’s economy will look like, but there will be an economy; it will just be different from 3 years ago.

I can do a lot alone, but any organization with a hundred people like me can do much, much more—and do it better.

And I wouldn’t be as effective and efficient in my work if I didn’t have 20 years of experience working in the IT industry and studying and implementing AI.

So, knowledge still rules, you just apply it not the way you used to.

Nice way to generate training data for building robotic models:

1. Go to this platform and define the experience your model needs.

2. They take that and define the tasks, settings, and movements.

3. Then, operators record real work. They wear cameras while completing the tasks you care about.

4. You get back a dataset with all of the recordings properly organized.

5. You can use that dataset to train your model.

items.title:
Some scientists are so trapped in the Dunning–Kruger effect; that's hilarious.

So, I see that a pap...
items.content:
Some scientists are so trapped in the Dunning–Kruger effect; that's hilarious.

So, I see that a paper's copyright belongs to the author, so I write to ask their permission to host a copy of it on ChapterPal.

The author: "You should ask arXiv!"

Me: "You hold the copyright, not arXiv, so I'm asking you."

The author: "But it's dumb to ask me about a single paper. Ask arXiv!"

Me: "This is how copyright law works, and there's nothing to ask arXiv about. Do you agree or not?"

Stops answering.
items.author: @burkov
items.summary: Burkov recounts an amusing exchange where a scientist author, whose copyright he sought to host a paper on ChapterPal, repeatedly insisted he ask arXiv instead despite arXiv holding no copyright, then stopped responding.
items.reasoning: Entertaining anecdote with a real point about copyright literacy among researchers; moderate engagement but limited broader significance.

I see mo...
items.content:
It's interesting every time I post about the issues with low quality immigration in Europe

I see most people on here agree

And then the only people that disagree keep coming back to this argument which apparently some people actually believe

"Europeans colonized the world, so now it's payback time and you're the one that should be colonized"

Of course that's ridiculous, you could go back in history to Genghis Khan and with that logic we should take over Mongolia right now to pay back for killing over 10% of the entire world's population in the 1200s

And even if the argument wouldn't be ridiculous, why would we just accept it?

But yes people actually see this as an argument to destroy Europe! Crazy!

items.title: Another awesome release on @ChapterPal: Lessons in Industrial Automation by Tony R. Kuphaldt (2018)....
items.content:
Another awesome release on @ChapterPal: Lessons in Industrial Automation by Tony R. Kuphaldt (2018).

Lessons in Industrial Automation by Tony R. Kuphaldt is a series of five textbook volumes for instrument technicians, process control specialists, automation engineers, and instructors. Requiring only basic algebra and physical intuition, it begins with fundamentals like electrical circuits, fluid mechanics, calculus, and chemistry, then moves on to measurement devices, analog and pneumatic signals, and digital networks such as Modbus and FOUNDATION Fieldbus.

The book’s core covers PID control, loop tuning, and advanced control strategies, along with relay logic, PLC programming, safety systems, calibration, and cybersecurity. Through hands-on procedures, readers learn to install, calibrate, program, and troubleshoot the devices found in modern processing facilities. It deliberately excludes topics like enterprise IT, robotics, and model predictive control, focusing instead on practical instrumentation and operational technology.

The five volumes altogether have 2,586 pages and 2,424 isllustrations, so veritually one illustration per page, and plenty of practical advice and real industrial settings photos.

All books on ChapterPal are free to read with a free account. It takes four minutes to wash my...
items.content:
@jchybow @j_grieshaber I actually timed my visits on a road trip. 

It takes four minutes to wash my windows. Which they need every few hours.

I need to get out and stretch. My legs are old and get numb if I don't.

I also need to pee every couple of hours. That takes four to six minutes.

I usually also want to get a drink or a snack. That can take one to three, depending if there is a line at the cashier.

And I'm not even figuring in going into a place and having lunch or dinner. 

Most of the time my car is ready to go when I get done with all that. 

It simply isn't a problem. At most on a long drive it adds another 30 minutes to the total trip (on an eight-hour drive from San Jose to Las Vegas, for instance).
